text: Opens with news anchors' audio about the indictment over aerial San Francisco shots; the end of the story (fraud charges) is given in the first 10 seconds.

Narrator restates the premise with numbers ($600M raised, $9B valuation) and promises the story of 'how it all came crashing down'; the closing question 'how did it go so horribly wrong' launches the story.
Knowing the ending does not kill curiosity: the open converts 'what happened' into 'how was this possible', the right question for a well-known scandal like Fyre.
Black title card 'Part One – Elizabeth and the rise of Theranos'; a second card 'Part Two – The truth always wins' appears around 17:38.
Estimated 25.5 visual changes per minute in the first two minutes (avg shot ~2.3 s), falling to ~18/min mid-video and ~15.5/min near the end.
Narrator explicitly flags the turning point: 'now this is the big lie' before explaining why the device could not work.

Explaining the technical impossibility before the scandal unfolds lets the viewer recognise every later lie; for Fyre the analogue is showing why the island, flights and housing could not work on that timeline.
Middle section alternates press photos, store footage (Walgreens check-in), document screenshots and interview clips; one exploded diagram of the miniLab appears near the end.
Emotional low point (death of chief scientist) placed at roughly 55 % of runtime, before the peak-of-fame section.
Peak of fame (Fortune cover, TED) is placed right before the investigation, maximising the contrast of the fall.
The reveal uses the real news segment about the WSJ article and the founder's TV interview as diegetic audio, then the narrator lists hard numbers (12 of 250 tests).
Music bed runs almost continuously under narration (measured median -19.5 dB, quiet <6 % of sampled time in all three windows).
About 4,300 words in 24:38 (~175 wpm) delivered by one narrator; narration gaps of 3 s or more occur only four times.
Ends with a reflective thesis (need to appear successful, repeated lies with credible names) and a counterfactual question before the channel outro.
The promo for other videos after the thesis dilutes the ending; for our format the last line should be the thesis or a callback to the cold open.
Thumbnail shows a tight portrait on a saturated pink field with the words 'THERANOS – THE FULL MOVIE'; the video title does not contain 'full movie'.
The thumbnail looks like a later repackaging for long-form viewing; we cannot see when it changed.
Sampled frames show highlighted document text and a quote card ('traditional machines bought from companies like Siemens') as visual support; no visible citation lines in sampled frames.
First line is the subject's own motivational slogan as archival audio, before the narrator speaks.
Childhood anecdote (wanting to be a billionaire), the rise in two sentences, then the twist that it was all a lie, and an explicit promise of 'why and how'.
Letting the subject's own promise open the video and immediately contradicting it is a compact 'promise vs. reality' hook that fits Fyre's promotional video vs. the tents.
Hook frames are desaturated black-and-white footage with animated red ink overlays and large keyword title cards that repeat the noun just spoken (name, 'The Secrets', 'Needles').
Every source type (stock, press photos, dramatised footage) is graded into the same red/black palette, giving a single visual identity across the video.
Many sampled frames appear to come from a dramatised TV/film production with actors, used as illustration without on-screen labelling.
Using fiction footage as illustration is a rights and accuracy risk we should not copy; reconstructions must be clearly ours and labelled.
Estimated 12 visual changes per minute in the first two minutes (avg ~4.8 s), 18.5/min mid-video, 16.5/min near the end.
A former employee's interview audio is inserted to confirm the fake investor demos ('who was doing the testing').
Mid-roll sponsor read at ~56 % of runtime, introduced right after a cliffhanger line about letting the public use the machines.
Narrator names the turning point explicitly: until now she had deceived investors, now she was putting the public at risk.
Part 1 ends on an open question ('how was she getting away with this') with an end-screen card to part 2.
Ending on the question instead of the answer suits a series; for a single Fyre video the same device works as an act break before the investigation section.
About 3,075 words in 15:40 (~196 wpm), faster than ColdFusion's ~175 wpm on the same topic; frequent rhetorical questions ('did this stop Elizabeth? absolutely not').
Music bed never drops out in sampled windows (median about -17.5 dB, 0 % quiet).
Thumbnail: subject's face with exaggerated eyes left, red ink splash and blood vial, one word 'FRAUD' in dripping red on white background.
One-word verdict plus a face and one object is legible at small size; the edited 'crazy eyes' face is a caricature we would avoid for real people.
Opens with a general statement about dreaming of success over a montage of business magazine covers, then names the subject and her honours.
Turns on 'behind this polished facade', inserts a news clip about possible prison time, and closes with the explicit question of who she was and how she fooled the bank.
The first 40 seconds are generic; the specific charge (fake customers) would be a stronger first line. Our hook should start on the most specific image.
Reveal is built as a gap: claimed 4.25M customers vs. under 300k real, followed by a 'crossroads' framing of her decision.
The fabrication is told as a heist sequence: an engineer refuses, an outside professor builds the fake list, the list is destroyed after analysis.
Discovery is shown through a concrete metric: of 400k marketing emails, few delivered and 1 % opened.
A single concrete, checkable number makes the fall feel inevitable; Fyre has equivalents (ticket price vs. delivered tent, FEMA tents, cheese sandwich photo).
After the verdict the narrator goes back to her early biography and shows those claims were also false, presenting it as 'what she had been doing all along'.
A second reveal after the main payoff keeps the last third alive and turns an event into a character study.
The founder's own TV pitch is played in her voice to explain the product, later contrasted with the fraud.
Estimated 20.5 visual changes per minute in the first two minutes, 19.5 mid-video, 13.5 near the end.
Black quote cards with italic white serif text are used for quotations from witnesses and the founder.
Closes with a thesis (fake it till you make it, Holmes and SBF parallels, easy-money era) and then the narrator's personal opinion about a generation.
Thumbnail: candid photo of the subject, text 'SHE STOLE $175 MILLION', red arrow pointing at her, small 'Whoops', channel logo.
Title and thumbnail split the information (age + victim in the title, amount in the thumbnail) so the pair reads as one sentence without repeating.
Opens on the end point (heading to Alcatraz), then says the crime that sent him there was not even his most infamous scam, then lands the title fact with a one-word sentence ('Twice').
Flash-forward plus 'and that wasn't even the worst part' creates two open loops in under 30 s; the callback at the end closes the first one.
After the promise there is an ~18 s music-only title sequence before the narration resumes.
Narrator states uncertainty openly: birth year 'most likely', identity unknown, at least 45 aliases.
Place names appear as large, lit 3D-style text composited into period photos (Alcatraz, Hostinné/Czech Republic, Prague).

The money-box con is explained as an ordered procedure (prepare notes, win trust, reluctant demo, 6-hour delay, bank check, victim offers to buy), with 'here's the clever part' and 'here's the real genius' markers.
Walking through the mechanism lets viewers feel smarter than the victims and explains why intelligent people fell for it; Fyre's investor and ticket mechanics can be told the same way.
Foreshadowing: when introducing the wife, the narrator says his personal life would be his downfall 'but we'll get to that'; the payoff arrives at 19:18.
Explains why victims stay silent (shame), and uses that to set up the second sale of the tower.
Sponsor segment placed at ~51 % between chapters 2 and 3; a subscribe request at ~73 %.
Ends with an ironic detail (death certificate lists him as 'apprentice salesman') then an end-screen link to a related video.
Several sampled frames are scenes from feature films with recognisable actors, used to illustrate events of the 1920s–30s.
About 4,440 words in 21:33 (~206 wpm).
Estimated 20 visual changes per minute in the first two minutes, 16 mid-video, 25.5 in the escape/arrest climax.
Thumbnail: masked hooded figure holding two Eiffel Towers with red '?' price tags and a banknote; no text and no image of the real person.
Visualising the absurd action from the title works when no good photo exists, but the hacker mask is a genre cliché unrelated to the era.
Opens in the first person: the narrator lists candidate words for the case (deceptive, brilliant, concerning, scary) and picks 'crazy', then states the thesis.
A personal, opinionated frame works for a host-like voice; for a faceless Czech narrator the same idea is a one-line verdict that the ending returns to.
Anchors scale with a familiar comparison (a zany version of Best Buy) and peak numbers (6th largest chain, ~4 % market, $350M sales).
Plays a few seconds of the original TV commercials so the viewer hears the hype before the fraud is explained.
A yellow slide listing the two eras (1970s tax evasion / lower profits; 1980s raise stock price / higher profits) appears and returns at least three times as a signpost.
Returning to the same agenda graphic gives a complex story a map; useful for Fyre's parallel threads (marketing, island logistics, ticket money, investors).
Counter-intuitive reveal: profits appeared to grow because they skimmed less, framed as 'committing a fraud by committing less fraud'.
Each accounting trick (fake invoices, inventory double counting, timing, comparable-store sales) gets its own example; scanned statements and simple bar charts are shown.
Estimated 7–8 visual changes per minute throughout (average shot ~7–8 s), the slowest of the sampled business channels so far.
Music bed sits lower (median about -23.5 dB) than in ColdFusion or MagnatesMedia (-17 to -19 dB); narration dominates.
Court-era interview clips of the two cousins accusing each other are inserted as dialogue.
Ends with personal reflection, the recovered money for investors, and a call to comment on which word fits, closing the opening loop.
Thumbnail uses the brand's own yellow and logo lettering, a cut-out of the founder giving a thumbs up, and a red 'SCANDAL' stamp.

Borrowing the subject's brand look makes the topic instantly recognisable to those who know it; Fyre's own promotional imagery (logo, turquoise sea, models on the beach) would be the equivalent, shown as quoted evidence, not reused as our branding.
Opens with an openly personal verdict about the subject before any facts.
Names the viewer's knowledge gap (heard of a Ponzi scheme but never quite understood it) and promises only a 'decent overview', lowering expectations honestly.
Role-play: the narrator pretends to be a well-off investor in 2004, gets a referral, meets the subject, receives steady 1 % monthly returns and feels honoured.
Explicit perspective switch ('that was my perspective as an investor, now let's look at what was actually happening'): no stocks bought, reports typed in the office.
Experiencing the scam from the victim's side first makes the reveal land and protects victims from looking stupid; this maps directly to Fyre ticket buyers in early 2017.
'How did he get away with it' is answered as a list: charisma, reputation, a believable 10–12 % return, consistency, official-looking paperwork, regulators ignoring the whistleblower.
An aside compares reputation-based trust to judging a film you have not seen, with a meme image on screen.
Collapse explained with the same mechanism set up earlier: in 2008 withdrawals exceeded new money.
Separates victims who were rich investors from ordinary people and charities, and says their only mistake was failing to spot a hard-to-spot fraud.
Pre-empts the obvious pun on the subject's name to stop it in the comments, turning it into a self-aware joke.
Estimated 5–7.5 visual changes per minute (average shot 7.5–11 s); stock clips match the role-play literally.
Thumbnail repeats the title text with a red 'SCANDAL' stamp and a cut-out photo; same template as other videos in the 'Simple Overview' series.
A series template builds recognition but adds no curiosity; better to put the one surprising fact in the thumbnail and the name in the title.
Opens with a reconstructed scene told in present tense: an employee gets a help-desk call, logs in, confirms 2FA; only then is the caller revealed.
Reveal of the caller via concrete status details (17 years old, white BMW, gemstone Rolex) and 'this one will be the biggest hack of his life'.
Starting inside a scene rather than with a summary makes the opening feel like a film; for Fyre the arrival of the first guests at the site is such a scene.
Hook frames are original 3D renders: stylised, faceless characters (masked or mannequin-like) in dark offices, close-ups of phones and login screens.
Across the video about 60 % of sampled frames are original 3D scenes; real photos appear only for public figures and news screenshots.
Stylised faceless 3D figures solve two problems at once: no likeness rights for private people and a recognisable, consistent look. This fits a Blender-based pipeline.
A side story about a different victim is told with the victim's own podcast audio, establishing the SIM-swap technique before the main event.
Sponsor read is bridged from the story ('everything he needed he taught himself') at ~32 % of runtime.
The day of the hack is divided into 'phase one/two/three', with an on-screen 1-2-3 counter highlighting the current phase.
The climax is told with exact clock times ('at exactly 4:17 p.m.') and follower counts for each hijacked account.
Chat messages and forum posts are shown as recreated UI cards and read aloud; a node-graph board links aliases to real names.
Narrator states the limit of knowledge ('we don't know exactly who LOL is, but the New York Times spoke with him').
Outcome for each crew member is listed, including unresolved ones; the hearing is described as hijacked by Zoom bombers.
Ends on a thesis: the mastermind was not a brilliant hacker; simple social engineering and massive reach were enough.
Music bed median about -22 dB, quieter than ColdFusion/MagnatesMedia; brief music-only beats before the shutdown (14:20, 14:44).
Thumbnail: game-style character with a pickaxe on a fire background, a large red 'Massive HACK' button with a cursor, small '$16,500,000' and 'case file sealed'.
The title's $16,500,000 figure does not appear in the transcript; the narration mentions up to $180,000 for the main suspect and other sums.
An unexplained headline number undermines trust in a fact-based channel; our titles should only use figures the script proves.
Opens on the hunt itself: police have been after her for 7 years, mostly for laptops holding the key; then a list of stakes and story elements.
The opening is a fast montage (estimated 36.5 visual changes per minute, avg ~1.6 s), slowing to ~14/min mid-video and ~11/min at the end.
Narrator says the biography is hard to piece together and names the main source (a China Newsweek profile).
Before the scheme, the video explains the social background (one-child policy, lonely elderly, new law on visiting parents) that made the victims receptive.
The con is laid out as labelled steps: 'Step one, the front', 'Step two, the plan', 'Step three, the promise', 'Step four, the scheme'.
Set-piece scene of a mass investor rally told in present tense: veiled leader in a wheelchair lifted above the crowd, chanting the company promise.
Investors are taken to see the 'mining warehouse'; the machines are off ('to avoid radiation'), and one visitor invests more afterwards.
A staged site visit that convinces visitors is a strong parallel to Fyre's promotional shoot on the island; showing what visitors saw versus what was there is the reveal.
Inserts an original interview with a Guardian journalist who covered the trial, describing the messages and the courtroom.
Real police bodycam audio of the first raid, with the subject claiming another name while lying in bed.
States that almost all investors refused interviews and that the one who agreed asked for help getting her money back.
Ends on an open, ironic line about investors possibly getting rich after all if compensation is approved.
Recurring style: thin white line diagrams on near-black with small photo badges for people, used for money flows and the pyramid structure.
A hand-drawn style map is used for Liberland; no satellite or 3D map in sampled frames.
Thumbnail is an unedited-looking police bodycam still of the subject in bed with a 'REC' overlay; no text.
A real 'caught' frame from authorities is more intriguing than a designed face; for Fyre the equivalent is a real attendee photo of the tents or the sandwich, with rights checked.
Player metadata title ('How China's Biggest Scammer Got Caught') differs from the page title ('The Insane Hunt for China's Biggest Scammer').
The two titles likely indicate an A/B title test; we cannot see which version is winning.
Opens on an ordinary supermarket and frames it as a paradox: one of the most isolated supermarkets on earth that does not look isolated.
A paradox about an everyday object invites the viewer to find the hidden system; Fyre equivalent: a luxury festival that needed every bottle of water shipped in.
Isolation is expressed through comparisons to known distances (as far from Los Angeles as New York, from Japan as Afghanistan) and flight times.
Hook visuals move from the store exterior up through clouds to a 3D globe showing the Pacific, then down to the islands.
The anomaly is introduced with one concrete price ($10 for a gallon of milk).
A specific ship's voyage (departure and arrival days, speeds out and back) illustrates the economics.
Item-by-item price comparison between two stores of the same chain (beef, cabbage, lemons, eggs).
Adds a risk scenario (tsunami or hurricane hitting the single port) before the historical turn.
Turn: 'it doesn't have to be this way – in fact, it wasn't', introduced through a tourist spot that is actually an ancient fishpond.
Revealing that a place tourists see has a hidden history is a reusable turn; for Fyre the beach used in the promo video vs. the gravel lot where the event took place.
Most sampled frames are filmed location footage (stores, ports, aerials) and satellite-style maps with routes; no character animation.
Estimated 10.5–12.5 visual changes per minute across the three windows (average shot ~4.6–5.5 s).
A closing note explains why the topic was hard to research fairly and how bias was avoided, before the sponsor.
Sponsor read is placed at the very end after the thesis, not mid-video.
Thumbnail: photoreal island and container ship, title text repeated in black boxes, channel logo and coloured stripe.
Literal thumbnails work for a channel with a strong brand and explanatory titles; for a new channel without that trust, a sharper curiosity gap is likely needed.
The first minute is a host note explaining that this video is the pilot of a new sister channel, before any story begins.
A minute of channel housekeeping before the hook likely costs retention; for Fyre the cold open should come first and any notes later.
Cold open in medias res: the final scheduled ferry leaves the island on a named date and hour, carrying the last holdouts.
A precise dated final moment creates a question the whole film answers; Fyre parallel: the evening of 27 April 2017 on Great Exuma.
A named former resident speaks in their own recorded voice, inserted into the narration rather than shown as a talking head throughout.
Interview recordings are framed inside a postcard-style graphic with a stamp and ruled lines instead of full-frame video.
A consistent graphic frame for testimony keeps a faceless film human and visually unified; we would design our own frame, not copy this one.
The history is told through one resource, the cod fishery, from abundance to collapse.
One through-line object keeps a long history readable; for Fyre the through-line could be the promise itself (the promo video) revisited at each stage.
A montage paragraph lists everyday life in the town, establishing what is about to be lost.
Black-and-white archival fishing footage and photos illustrate the historical sections.
The collapse is supported by the interviewee's first-hand account of travelling far north and still finding no fish under a moratorium.
The first resettlement vote, 85 for and 10 against, missed the required threshold by a fraction of a percent; the second vote was unanimous.
The vote is shown on a flat map with a simple bar chart and the number.
Exact numbers turn a procedural moment into a near-miss with tension; Fyre equivalents are dated deadlines and payments missed.
The film returns to the departing ferry from the opening, now with the history known.
The callback closes the loop opened in the cold open and gives the ending emotional weight.
The closing thesis generalises: remote settlements cannot exist in a vacuum.
Estimated 9.5 cuts per minute in the first two minutes, 10.5 in the middle and 7.5 near the end.
Median audio level in measured windows was about -27 to -30 dB, quieter than the main Wendover video measured earlier.
Narration pauses of several seconds occur at 0:58, 7:27, 8:28, 13:24 and 19:21, letting footage and testimony breathe.
Illustrated vintage postcard of a red fishing shed and boat with the place name in postcard lettering.
The thumbnail names the place and sets a mood; the dated mystery lives only in the title, so the two divide the work.
The video opens with a one-sentence premise: a person sold paintings worth millions, and all were fake.
A dated 1995 case follows a collector's doubt to a lab test and a police dead end, then closes on 'the very tip of the iceberg'.
Starting from the investigators' failure and then cutting to the culprit gives dramatic irony: the viewer knows more than the police.
The narrator explicitly separates documented history from the invented provenance story.
Saying aloud where the truth ends and the lie begins builds trust and teaches the viewer how the con worked; useful for Fyre's island marketing claims.
The forger's method is explained as deliberate choices: invent new works by prolific artists rather than copy famous ones.
The subjects' own version is reported: they deny fleeing and cite a child's illness.
A sponsor read sits at about 9:33, bridged from the story with a sentence about systems working together.
The staged 'grandmother' photograph is shown, then each painting in it is identified as a forgery.
Showing and annotating the actual forged exhibit is the strongest proof moment in the video; Fyre has equivalent exhibits in the promo video and pitch materials.
The turn comes from a mundane request: a buyer asks for a certificate that does not exist.
A pigment anachronism exposes the forger again, echoing the 1995 case.
Planting a detail in the hook and paying it off later rewards attention without a flash-forward.
The cover story is undone by its internal contradictions: the supposed protector was a teenager and later joined the Nazi Party.
Most scenes are stylised illustrated re-enactments of real people with slow camera moves, not real footage.
Illustrated re-enactment of real people shows undocumented moments but is not labelled as dramatised; we should mark re-enactment explicitly.
A recurring cast map shows people as portrait circles on black with name captions, added as they enter.
A dark map of Europe with highlighted countries shows the move to France and the police's cross-border problem.
Real photographs and TV interview footage of the subjects appear mainly in the aftermath section.
Measured only about 5 cuts per minute in the opening and 12 near the end; slow moves inside illustrations are not counted.
Median audio level about -20 dB with almost no quiet passages; the captions label music moods changing with each beat.
An auction is re-enacted with an auctioneer's bidding calls and a gavel sound.
The ending leaves an open moral question instead of a downfall.
Rendered auctioneer points at a colourful painting under a ten-million-dollar sign; the word 'fake' with an arrow labels it.
The thumbnail delivers the twist and a price, while the title supplies scale; the specific dollar figure is not tied to one sale in the narration.
The video opens with a montage of TV news audio announcing the explosion and the spill before any narration of its own.
News voices establish scale and authenticity in seconds; for Fyre, contemporary news and social posts from 27-28 April 2017 could play the same role if licensed or cited.
The narrator states two goals: tell the race to stop the spill and visualise how much oil was lost beyond numbers.
A 3D Empire State Building is introduced as an empty measuring container that fills as the leak continues.
A single running visual measure that returns at every phase makes an abstract quantity cumulative and memorable.
Schedule delay and daily operating cost are given as context for the decision to continue despite warning signs.
The company's first statement that no oil was leaking is reported and then the correction a few days later.
Equipment is explained with clean 3D models in a neutral pale-blue and sand space rather than realistic sea-floor scenes.
A neutral 'lab room' style keeps technical explanation readable and is cheap to reuse across scenes; suitable for a Blender pipeline.
The middle is a sequence of attempts labelled as plans: relief wells, a dome, a pipe, a junk shot and caps, most failing.
Repeated attempt and failure is a natural tension engine; Fyre's organisers also tried a series of fixes before cancellation.
Black cards with a day number (for example DAY 36, DAY 82) mark the passage of time between phases.
The final fix first required cutting the pipe, which was expected to increase the flow by up to 20 %.
The official volume and a higher independent estimate are both given, with the company's objection and its stated interest in the lower figure.
Presenting competing figures with each source's interest is a model for Fyre's disputed numbers (tickets sold, money lost).
The last two minutes promote the creator's subscription platform and next video.
About 14.5 cuts per minute in the opening news montage, about 5 in the 3D middle and 18.5 in the promotional ending.
Median level about -18 to -21 dB in all windows with almost no quiet passages.
The thumbnail is a photoreal burning platform with a smoke column on calm sea and no text.
For a famous event, the defining image alone can carry the thumbnail; Fyre's defining image is the disaster-relief tents or the sandwich.
The hook narrates the descent in sequence, adding depth, minutes and atmospheres of pressure step by step.
Accumulating numbers turn a technical fact into suspense even when the ending is known; a Fyre parallel is the countdown of days and missing tents.
After contact is lost the narrator states the failure could have been predicted and that experts did predict it.
The narrator states his own background as a composite design engineer before the analysis.
The video limits its scope to one design aspect, the composite hull, and dismisses side issues explicitly.
The company's own blog post rejecting classification is quoted at length as the main exhibit.
The subject's own public words are harder to dispute than outside criticism; Fyre has the promo video, pitch materials and posts.
Quoted documents are shown printed on paper with yellow highlighter on the key lines.
A 2022 review paper is cited and quoted to show the failure mode was poorly understood.
The hull manufacturer's 2017 trade interview is quoted and the vagueness of 'less than 1 % voids' questioned.
A 2018 court case shows an employee who raised hull concerns was fired.
A visiting expert heard cracking on a test dive and warned the CEO, who ignored it.
An analogy explains why acoustic monitoring could not warn in time (seeing lightning before thunder).
The narration uses strong judgement words about the CEO, such as 'narcissistic' and 'death trap'.
Loaded words weaken an otherwise documented argument and raise legal risk; for Fyre the documents should carry the judgement.
The opening frames show an evidence board with pinned printouts and red strings, a motif repeated around 11:38.
About 14.5 cuts per minute in the opening, about 11 in the middle and end windows.
Median audio level about -24 dB with almost no quiet passages.
Rendered submersible in deep blue water with 'DOOMED TO FAIL?' and a yellow arrow pointing at the hull.
The question form in the thumbnail invites a verdict while the title signals analysis; the arrow points at the exact failed part.
The cold open is a timeline with clock times, crew experience and take-off call-outs, ending with the bang and the crash.
Precise clock times create a documentary feel and slow time down before the event; Fyre could open on the hours of 27 April 2017.
The narrator frames the video as the story of a multi-year investigation using engineering.
Each section ends on an explicit unanswered question that the next section takes up.
Three runway items are introduced as clues: the tyre, a metal strip with irregular holes and an unburned tank piece.
Planting three clues early and resolving them one by one keeps a long technical explanation driven by curiosity.
Maintenance records trace the strip to an aircraft that departed five minutes earlier.
A physical test with a weighted wagon confirms the strip cuts the tyre as in the debris.
A complication rules out the easy answer: 57 earlier tyre failures and a 1979 tank puncture caused no fire.
The fuel leak rate is estimated from flame dimensions in photos and confirmed by a surviving fuel gauge.
The official report is quoted on the fracture surface, followed by a materials explanation.
The full causal chain is recapped in one paragraph.
A recurring desk scene shows pinned photos, report pages and maps connected with string, filmed with shallow focus.
A single recurring evidence space gives a faceless investigation a visual home; our version should use our own documents and design.
About 14.5 cuts per minute in all three measured windows; the pace is even rather than front-loaded.
Median audio level about -24 dB in all windows.
The aircraft trailing flame with hand-drawn circles and a question mark, text 'SOLVING AN ENGINEERING MYSTERY'.
Hand-drawn annotation points the eye to the mystery; title and thumbnail split the promise into truth and puzzle.
The video starts with a one-line sponsor mention before the story.
The hook lists daily-life consequences of inflation: queuing for an ATM from 2 a.m., bread costing billions, vending machines out of service.
Absurd everyday details make an abstract economic figure tangible within seconds; for Fyre, the promised versus delivered meal or bed works the same way.
The hook ends on the largest banknote, one hundred trillion dollars, worth about 40 US cents.
A two-part question promises both the cause and an unexpected consequence, the rise of mobile money.
Before the history, a short portrait of the country's natural wonders sets up what is lost.
Money printing is explained with a simple rule and an ironic concrete detail: banknotes ordered from abroad were worthless on arrival.
ATM density per 100,000 people is compared across countries to show how unbanked the region is.
Most explanations use flat vector icons and flags on a light dotted background, built up piece by piece.
A small flat-icon vocabulary is cheap to produce and keeps money flows readable; useful for Fyre's investor and vendor money trail.
An exchange-rate line chart with a sharply rising curve illustrates the inflation.
The thesis reframes the crisis: the challenges were the ingredients for innovation.
About 11.5 cuts per minute at the start, dropping to about 4 in the final window.
Median audio level about -22 to -24 dB with few quiet passages.
Flag-colour stripes, savanna silhouettes, a highlighted Africa map and the title text in black and yellow bars.
The thumbnail relies on the title text rather than a striking image; the bill itself is not shown.
The hook opens on a small concrete detail: exams cancelled because schools could not afford paper and ink.
A small, surprising concrete detail signals a large collapse more vividly than a statistic; Fyre has similar details.
The hook escalates to prices, power cuts and protests, then widens to a global warning quoted from the UN.
An imaginary country is used to explain trade deficits and dollar supply before returning to the real case.
Teaching the mechanism on a neutral model first lets the real case land without jargon; useful for festival cash flow.
The overvalued currency is explained with an everyday example of a bank paying 150 and a shop paying 200 for one dollar.
The crisis is summarised as three interconnected problems, numbered on screen.
A popular explanation is checked: only about 10 % of the debt is owed to China.
Explicitly testing a popular explanation builds credibility; Fyre has its own popular myths to test.
The narrator explains that one country was chosen to humanise what are otherwise numbers on a graph.
In the sponsor read the narrator says many clips in the video came from a licensed stock library and shows the search results.
Licensed stock is a legal footage base for a faceless channel; we would check each licence before use.
All charts and icon graphics share one red colour theme with white and yellow labels.
About 5.5 cuts per minute in the opening, 7 in the middle and 14 near the end.
Median audio level about -18 to -20 dB with almost no quiet passages.
Red background, falling candlestick chart, the island in orange and the text 'WHY SRI LANKA'S ECONOMY IS COLLAPSING'.
The hook gives the known facts and the persisting doubt in about 40 seconds, with no dramatisation.
The narrator explicitly narrows the scope to events inside one building.
A stated narrow scope signals depth and honesty about limits; the Fyre pilot can promise a precise slice instead of the whole saga.
